Patient demographics:

  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Kaito's life changed forever on a sweltering summer evening three years ago. He was working late at the bank in downtown Manhattan when a terrorist attack shook the city. Gunfire erupted outside, and Kaito watched in horror as people ran for cover, screaming and bleeding. The sounds of shattering glass and crumbling concrete still echoed in his mind. In the chaos, he had managed to hide under his desk, but the feeling of powerlessness lingered. In the aftermath, Kaito became withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and intimate relationships. He told himself it was because he didn't want to burden others with his problems, but deep down, he feared getting close to people would make him vulnerable again. His divorce from his high school sweetheart a year after the attack seemed like a natural consequence of this emotional numbing. They had grown apart, and Kaito couldn't shake off the feeling that he was no longer capable of being the partner she needed. As time passed, Kaito found solace in overwork. He would often volunteer for extra shifts or take on additional responsibilities to avoid being alone with his thoughts. His colleagues praised his dedication, but they began to notice a change in him – the irritability, the short fuse that would ignite at the slightest provocation. One day, he lashed out at a customer who had asked him a simple question, reducing the poor woman to tears. The incident left Kaito shaken, and he started wondering if he was losing control. At night, Kaito's sleep was fitful, punctuated by waking moments when he would sit up with a start, his heart racing, as he checked whether he was safe. He would get out of bed to scan the room, ensuring that no one was lurking in the shadows. This behavior had become so ingrained that even during the day, he found himself frequently looking behind him, checking if someone was following him. Kaito's self-perception had taken a hit as well. He felt like he had acted against his own values by hiding under the desk instead of trying to help others during the attack. The guilt still lingered, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that he wasn't trustworthy. When confronted with difficult decisions at work or in his personal life, Kaito would second-guess himself, wondering if he was truly capable of making sound judgments. Despite his best efforts to suppress thoughts about the trauma, fragments of that day continued to seep into his consciousness. He would see a news report about terrorism, and suddenly he was back under the desk, reliving the horror. The memories were no longer just painful reminders; they had become a threat, a constant reminder of his own vulnerability. Kaito's relationships with his family and friends began to fray as well. They expressed concern about his behavior, but he pushed them away, convinced that he was beyond help. His job performance started to suffer too, as the irritability and lack of focus took their toll. It was then that Kaito realized he needed professional help. With a sense of trepidation, Kaito scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping to finally confront the demons that had haunted him for so long. As he sat in the waiting room, flipping through a worn copy of People magazine, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was taking a step into the unknown – and that it might just be his only chance at redemption.
